content: A retroverted uterus, also known as a tilted or tipped uterus, refers to a uterus that is angled backward toward the spine rather than forward. This is in contrast to the more common anteverted uterus, which is tilted forward toward the bladder, with the anterior end slightly concave. Approximately one in three to five women, depending on the source, have a retroverted uterus. The term retroverted uterus should be distinguished from other positional variations of the uterus. For example, a retrocessed uterus describes a condition where both the superior and inferior ends of the uterus are pushed posteriorly. A severely anteflexed uterus refers to a uterus that bends in the same direction as a normal anteverted uterus (with the concave side anterior), but the bend is much more pronounced. A vertical uterus, on the other hand, describes a uterus where the fundus (the top of the uterus) is oriented straight upward. In most cases, a retroverted uterus is congenital, meaning it is present from birth. However, it can also result from pelvic surgery, pelvic adhesions, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, or complications from childbirth. Diagnosis of a retroverted uterus is typically made during a routine pelvic examination. While this condition usually does not cause medical problems, it can sometimes be associated with dyspareunia (pain during sexual intercourse) and dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation). For example, in one patient, imaging studies such as ultrasound and MRI confirmed the presence of a retroverted uterus. The position of the uterus does not affect fertility. During pregnancy, a retroverted uterus usually corrects itself by the 10th to 12th week of gestation. However, in rare cases, the uterus may remain retroverted, a condition referred to as persistent retroflexion. Persistent retroflexion of the pregnant uterus is incompatible with advanced pregnancy. If spontaneous or artificial repositioning does not occur, the patient may either experience a miscarriage or develop symptoms related to uterine incarceration before the end of the fourth month of pregnancy. In exceptional cases, pregnancy may continue, leading to uterine sacculation. In such instances, spontaneous delivery is impossible, and uterine rupture may occur. Treatment for a retroverted uterus is rarely necessary. When required, options include specific exercises, the use of a pessary, manual repositioning, or surgical intervention.
